protocols.name: Colour language
protocols.intent: Make the human's own ink a machine-readable semantic layer, so meaning is tagged with one stroke and recovered by a camera.
protocols.guidance: Fixed and universal across every artifact. Letter-first so it survives mono printing. Blue is reserved for questions to the AI. The human is the colour; the printer never prints meaning-bearing colour.

claims.claim: Colour-coding items by category speeds finding the items of a target category and improves accuracy, compared with uncoded material, when the reader knows the code. The benefit falls as the number of colours grows.

Coding a category in two channels at once, colour plus letter or glyph, keeps it identifiable when one channel fails (colour-vision deficiency, poor light, a mono print or photo) and improves identification over colour alone.
claims.construct: redundant coding (redundancy gain); accessibility of colour use

sources.cite: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.1 "Use of Color" (2018)

claims.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
claims.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

grounding.helps: when the ink colours carry a small, fixed set of meanings the reader already knows, and each role also carries its letter, so the meaning survives a mono print, colour-blindness or a bad photo
grounding.backfires: when there are more colours than a reader can reliably tell apart, when the letter is skipped once coloured pens are to hand, or when marking in colour is mistaken for learning rather than a way to find things again: colour coding helps search under some conditions and hurts under others

protocols.name: Confidence dots
protocols.intent: Rate certainty almost effortlessly, in a form that survives colour-blindness and bad photos.
protocols.guidance: A dot plus a glyph: high = filled dot + plus, medium = half dot + tilde, low = hollow dot + exclamation. Never encode high-stakes confidence in red-vs-green alone.

claims.claim: Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.

Coding a category in two channels at once, colour plus letter or glyph, keeps it identifiable when one channel fails (colour-vision deficiency, poor light, a mono print or photo) and improves identification over colour alone.
claims.construct: redundant coding (redundancy gain); accessibility of colour use

sources.cite: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.1 "Use of Color" (2018)

claims.claim: Errors a person made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected on a later test, once feedback is seen, than errors made with low confidence.

grounding.helps: when many items need a quick certainty mark so the agent can see where doubt lies; confidence tracks accuracy above chance in general, but a three-level dot scale is untested, so read the dots as relative flags, not probabilities
grounding.backfires: when a high dot is taken as settled, since excess certainty persists even where other overconfidence fades, or when the mark relies on colour alone and is lost to colour-blindness or a poor photo

protocols.name: Structural marks
protocols.intent: Carry relations and intent that words on a page can't express in the flow of thinking.
protocols.guidance: Circle = commit. Cross = rejected but kept visible (dead ends are evidence). Arrow = leads to / causes. Box = this is a decision. Margin question mark = revisit. Margin exclamation = important.

protocols.name: Page IDs
protocols.intent: Give every page a stable name so a photo can be mapped to its reading rules before it is interpreted.
protocols.guidance: A short id like W1-P3 in a large monospace face in the page header and on the return checklist. The AI reads the id first and applies that archetype's read-back rules.

protocols.name: Proof actions
protocols.intent: On a Proof, each colour role triggers an action when the page comes back.
protocols.guidance: Ask → answer · Stop → challenge the claim · Keep → go deeper · Crux → re-centre around it · Maybe → explore alternatives · Sense → justify the reasoning · Draft → apply the edit as written · ✕ → cut · ○ → lock. Research-cost actions wait for confirmation.

claims.claim: A fixed, shared set of marks, each mapped to one editing action, is used reliably by writers and editors to communicate corrections on paper.
claims.construct: proofreaders' marks as a mark → action convention

claims.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
claims.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

grounding.helps: when every mark keeps one meaning on every page, following the long practice of proofreaders' marks; whether fixed marks are used reliably has not been tested
grounding.backfires: when a mark's or colour's meaning shifts between pages or contexts, which invites mode errors even in trained users
